I'm kinda torn on this one. There is a huge part of me that completely disagrees with how this researcher attempted to facilitate very important critical security data. According to his own statement, he used "“Not being a customer, I wouldn’t have known where to send it, or whether they’d even reply to me" as his excuse for informing the big bad internet AND posting his Proof of Concept. I didnt say he exposed user data. He put users at risk by posting his Proof of Concept on Twitter. I agree, Responsible companies do have security teams, however, as you know, computer security is a massive beast that has to have input from independent researchers. (hence the popular bug bounty programs) Should this company have one? Yes, do they have one? I dont know. He doesnt either because he didnt bother to contact anyone. <--His own words remember) According to the article, this chap felt dissed at a conference because the "sales" guys at the booth didn't know what the fuck he was talking about and likely didnt answer his "What about security" question effectively. His response, "okay then...I'll show you I'm important." This is childish and unprofessional...in my opinion of course.

Maybe. But the long-established precedent even for white hat hackers is to give the company a reasonable amount of time to respond to a security concern, then publish it. Maybe this researcher wouldn't have done that if he had the opportunity, but since there was no way to tell this company about security problems, it's a moot question.

If you google "impero software security contact", you get nothing but a page saying, "is it safe? The answer is ‘yes.’"

Whereas if you google similar terms for microsoft, adobe, SAP, or just about any other company that takes computer security seriously, you get a page to report a vulnerability.

If you don't have a page to report vulnerabilities, that means you don't care about them. Since Impero clearly does not give a flying fuck about exposing its users data, why is it a third party's job to try to impress upon them the importance of it? It isn't.

At some point if you send out claims of intellectual property that don't hold up in court, you should lose that property into the public domain. That kind of penalty is the only thing that will give bad actors some pause when they asset rights they don't have.
